summary: Describes version 3 of the Layer Two Tunneling Protocol (L2TPv3). It defines the base control protocol and an encapsulation for tunneling multiple Layer 2 connections between two IP nodes. Separate documents give the details for each link type being emulated.

plainLanguage.summary: L2TPv3 carries Layer 2 traffic between two endpoints across an IP network. A control connection manages separate sessions, while companion specifications describe how each kind of traffic is carried.

subtitle: A control protocol and data format for carrying multiple Layer 2 connections across an IP network.

tldr.problem: Different Layer 2 circuits need to cross packet networks, but the earlier L2TP specification was closely tied to PPP.
tldr.mechanism: L2TPv3 sets up sessions over a reliable control channel and carries circuit frames in data messages identified by a 32-bit Session ID.
tldr.outcome: The base protocol is independent of the emulated link type. RFC 3931 has been updated by RFC 5641 and RFC 9601.

today: RFC 3931 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 5641 and RFC 9601.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 3931 defines version 3 of the Layer Two Tunneling Protocol (L2TP). It carries Layer 2 circuits across a packet network and separates the base protocol from the kind of Layer 2 traffic being carried. Companion documents specify details for individual pseudowire types, such as PPP, Ethernet, and Frame Relay.

The protocol has a control part that creates, maintains, and ends sessions, plus data encapsulation that carries circuit traffic between two L2TP nodes. The data channel can be used with or without the control channel when another method supplies session information.
sections.plainLanguage: L2TPv3 carries Layer 2 connections across a packet network. Other specifications explain the details for each type of connection.

sections.title: Endpoints, Connections and Sessions
sections.content:
The protocol runs between two L2TP Control Connection Endpoints (LCCEs). An LCCE is called an Access Concentrator (LAC) when it connects a session to a data link, and a Network Server (LNS) when it ends a session and processes the network-layer packet. One endpoint may serve either role for different sessions.

A reliable control connection can manage multiple sessions, and each session carries one emulated Layer 2 connection. L2TP supports LAC-to-LNS, LAC-to-LAC, and LNS-to-LNS arrangements. In a LAC-to-LAC arrangement, either endpoint may initiate a session.
sections.plainLanguage: Two endpoints first establish a control connection. They can then create separate sessions for the Layer 2 traffic they need to carry.

sections.title: Control and Data Messages
sections.content:
L2TP uses control messages to establish and maintain connections and sessions. These messages use reliable delivery. Data messages carry the tunneled Layer 2 traffic over an unreliable channel and are not retransmitted when lost.

A control header includes sequence numbers and a Control Connection ID. A data message contains a session header, an optional Layer 2-specific sublayer, and the tunneled payload. Control message bodies use Attribute Value Pairs (AVPs), which identify their values and may mark an AVP as mandatory or hidden.
sections.plainLanguage: Control messages manage the connection and are retransmitted when needed. Data messages carry the actual traffic, but L2TP does not retransmit lost data messages.

sections.title: Carrying Traffic over IP
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support L2TP directly over IP, using IP protocol number 115. They SHOULD also support L2TP over UDP, which can make traversal of NATs and firewalls easier. UDP control messages use port 1701, and their UDP checksums MUST be enabled; checksums for data messages MAY be disabled.

Each data session has a 32-bit Session ID and may have a Cookie of up to 64 bits. A receiver uses the Session ID to find the session and checks any Cookie associated with it. It MUST drop data with an invalid Session ID or Cookie. Implementations MUST support at least one method for handling mismatched MTUs.
sections.plainLanguage: The Session ID tells the receiver which session carries a packet. The receiver checks the session details and drops packets that do not match.

sections.title: Reliable Control and Keepalives
sections.content:
Control messages use a sliding window with sequence numbers so a receiver can detect duplicates and deliver messages in order. If a message is not acknowledged, the sender retransmits it. The recommended initial retransmission timer is 1 second; later retransmissions use exponential backoff. If the peer does not respond after a configurable number of attempts, the connection and its sessions are cleared.

An LCCE sends a Hello control message when it has received no data or control traffic from its peer for a period of time. The recommended default is 60 seconds and MUST be configurable. Failure to deliver a Hello reliably causes the sender to declare the control connection down.
sections.plainLanguage: The endpoints confirm control messages and resend them if confirmation does not arrive. A Hello message checks whether the other endpoint is still reachable.

sections.title: Authentication and Data Protection
sections.content:
Control Message Authentication is optional. When used, it checks a hash over the entire control message using a shared secret and random values from both endpoints. It authenticates both endpoints, checks message integrity, and helps prevent spoofing and replay. Both endpoints must use the mechanism or neither does.

The data channel does not provide cryptographic security. If L2TP crosses a public or untrusted IP network and privacy or protection from sophisticated attacks is needed, IPsec MUST be made available. A Cookie does not replace IPsec when an attacker can observe and correlate packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Endpoints can authenticate and check control messages with a shared secret. L2TP does not encrypt data traffic, so IPsec is needed when that traffic requires protection on an untrusted network.
